greek: Ἐλθὼν δὲ Ιωσηφ ἀπήγγειλεν τῷ Φαραω λέγων Ὁ πατήρ μου καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί μου καὶ τὰ κτήνη καὶ οἱ βόες αὐτῶν καὶ πάντα τὰ αὐτῶν ἦλθον ἐκ γῆς Χανααν καὶ ἰδού εἰσιν ἐν γῇ Γεσεμ.
hint: Joseph tells Pharaoh that his father and brothers have come from Canaan with their flocks and are in Gesem.

notes.text: Plural, with the whole list for its subject: the father, the brothers, the flocks and herds, the oxen and all their things came.

greek: εἶπεν δὲ Φαραω τῷ Ιωσηφ Κατοικείτωσαν ἐν γῇ Γεσεμ· εἰ δὲ ἐπίστῃ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἄνδρες δυνατοί, κατάστησον αὐτοὺς ἄρχοντας τῶν ἐμῶν κτηνῶν. Ἦλθον δὲ εἰς Αἴγυπτον πρὸς Ιωσηφ Ιακωβ καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἤκουσεν Φαραω βασιλεὺς Αἰγύπτου. καὶ εἶπεν Φαραω πρὸς Ιωσηφ λέγων Ὁ πατήρ σου καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί σου ἥκασι πρὸς σέ·
hint: Pharaoh lets them dwell in Gesem and offers able men a post over his cattle; then he hears that Jacob has come.

notes.text: The Greek orders 47:5–6 otherwise than the Hebrew. Pharaoh's answer about Goshen and the able men comes first; then a sentence the Hebrew lacks, that Jacob and his sons came to Egypt and Pharaoh heard; then the words the Hebrew gives first, your father and brothers have come to you.
Present indicative of ἐπίσταμαι, to know how and to know for certain: if you know that there are able men among them.
δυνατός is strong, able, powerful: men of capacity, not only of strength.
The perfect of ἥκω again, as at 46:31: they have come, and are here.
The digital module spells this Ιωσηφ as Ιωσφη; the printed page has Ιωσηφ, and the transcription follows the page, listing it in `printed`.

greek: ἰδοὺ ἡ γῆ Αἰγύπτου ἐναντίον σού ἐστιν· ἐν τῇ βελτίστῃ γῇ κατοίκισον τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου.
hint: Pharaoh puts the land of Egypt before Joseph and tells him to settle his father and brothers in the best of it.

notes.text: βέλτιστος, the superlative of good: in the best land, the land at its best. The Hebrew has bĕmêṭab hāʾāreṣ, in the best of the land.
κατοικίζω, the causative: make them dwell, settle them. Middle Liddell's first sense is to remove to a place.
The Hebrew goes on, let them dwell in the land of Goshen, and if you know able men among them; the Greek has said both already, at 47:5.

hint: Jacob counts a hundred and thirty years of sojourning, few and hard, short of his fathers' years.

notes.text: The days which I sojourn: παροικέω again, where the Hebrew has the noun mĕgûray, my sojournings. Jacob counts his whole life as a resident alien's.

Perfect of γίνομαι: have come to be, and stand so.

hint: The people tell Joseph he has saved them, and that they will be Pharaoh's servants.

notes.text: You have saved us, and we stand saved: σῴζω, where the Hebrew has heḥĕyitānû, you have kept us alive.
We found favour, an aorist indicative. The Hebrew has the wish nimṣāʾ-ḥēn, may we find favour.

hint: Joseph makes it an ordinance to this day that a fifth of Egypt's produce goes to Pharaoh; only the priests' land is not his.

notes.text: The present infinitive of ἀποπεμπτόω, to give a fifth part of: the -οῦν of a verb in -όω. The same verb as Joseph's counsel at 41:34.
It was not Pharaoh's: the dative of possession.

hint: Israel settles in Egypt, in Gesem; they gain holdings there and grow and multiply greatly.

notes.text: κληρονομέω is to receive a share of an inheritance: an allotment as heirs. The Hebrew has wayyēʾāḥăzû, they took holdings.
The singular for Israel the man, then the plural for Israel the people.

hint: Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt, and his whole life comes to a hundred and forty-seven years.

notes.text: ἐπιζάω is to live on, to survive: he lived on in Egypt. The Hebrew has the plain wayĕḥî, he lived.
ἐνιαυτός is any long period, a cycle, and so a year: the days of Jacob of the years of his life.

notes.text: Pity and truth, for the Hebrew ḥesed weʾĕmet, kindness and faithfulness. ἐλεημοσύνη is the word later used for alms.
The articular infinitive, in the genitive: so as not to bury me.

greek: εἶπεν δέ Ὄμοσόν μοι. καὶ ὤμοσεν αὐτῷ. καὶ προσεκύνησεν Ισραηλ ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ.
hint: Israel makes Joseph swear; Joseph swears, and Israel bows down upon the top of his staff.

notes.text: Of the staff. The Hebrew consonants mṭh are read mîṭṭâ, bed, in the Masoretic text: Israel bowed at the head of the bed. The Greek reads maṭṭeh, staff. Hebrews 11:21 quotes the Greek.
Rahlfs prints δέ with its acute before the capital of the direct speech, not the grave.
προσκυνέω, to make obeisance, to prostrate oneself: an act of the body.
